p090.lead: The age of medicine men, shamans, and priests who stood as intermediaries between man and God—their tricks and their medicine, the burden and the contribution of their rituals.

p090.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p090.s0.h: Introduction — The Long Age Between Fear and Love
p090.s0.b0: Paper 90 asks who conducted the primitive observances described in the three preceding papers. Its author, a Melchizedek of Nebadon, explains that religious observance progressed from placation, avoidance, exorcism, and coercion to sacrifice, atonement, and redemption, and that as ritual grew more complex it was inevitably dominated by medicine men, shamans, and priests.
p090.s0.b1: In time the spirit world came to be regarded as unresponsive to the ordinary mortal. Once people believed that only exceptional men and women could catch the ear of the gods, religion entered a secondhand phase. The author adds that most of the organized religious systems on Urantia today are still passing through this level.
p090.s0.b3: The paper’s whole frame is set out in the last paragraph of its introduction. Evolutionary religion is born of a simple, all-powerful fear that surges through the mind before the unknown, and it eventually reaches the realization of an all-powerful love—the limitless affection of the Universal Father for the sons of the universe. Between that beginning and that consummation lie the long ages of the shamans, who presumed to stand between man and God as intermediaries.
p090.s1.h: I. The First Shamans — The Medicine Men
p090.s1.b0: The shaman was the ranking medicine man, the ceremonial fetishman, and the focus personality for all the practices of evolutionary religion. In many groups he outranked the war chief, marking the beginning of the church’s domination of the state. Often the office was hereditary.
p090.s1.b1: Because anything abnormal was ascribed to spirit possession, any striking mental or physical abnormality qualified a person to become a medicine man. Many of the men were epileptic and many of the women hysteric, and the author holds that these two types account for a good deal of ancient inspiration and possession. Most shamans sincerely believed they were possessed by spirits, but many were shrewd and able tricksters.

p090.s1.b3: In the end a shaman’s reputation rested on apparent achievement. If he failed and could not offer a plausible alibi, he was demoted or killed. The result was a paradox.
p090.s1.b5: Shamanism took the direction of tribal affairs out of the hands of the old and the strong and lodged it in the hands of the shrewd, the clever, and the farsighted. This shift of power from strength to wit was itself a kind of change.
p090.s2.h: II. Shamanistic Practices — Seekers of Revelation and Their Price
p090.s2.b0: Spirit conjuring was a precise and highly complicated procedure, comparable to church rituals conducted in an ancient tongue. Mankind sought superhuman help—revelation—very early, and people believed the shaman actually received it. Shamans relied heavily on the power of suggestion, but almost always negative suggestion; positive suggestion has been used only in very recent times. Their chief function was not so much healing disease as knowing and controlling the hazards of living.
p090.s2.b1: The same art was called white art when practiced by priests or shamans and black art when practiced by others. Later the witch became associated with the devil, setting the stage for comparatively recent outbreaks of religious intolerance. Shamans believed that chance revealed the will of the spirits and so cast lots, a habit that survives in children’s “counting-out” rhymes.
p090.s2.b3: Astrology, dream interpreting, and the rain makers or weather shamans all come down from ancient times. The Caesars banished the astrologers again and again, yet popular belief always brought them back, and thousands still believe in lucky and unlucky stars. In every age, though, true prophets and teachers arose to expose shamanism—among them the Shawnee Tenskwatawa, who predicted the eclipse of 1806 and denounced the vices of the white man.
p090.s2.b4: Shamanism was not confined to any one region. The Greeks believed in oracles, the Chinese used magic against demons, and shamanism flourished in India; across much of the world it was abandoned only recently. The paper invites us to read it not as the failing of one people but as a stage the whole human race has passed through.
p090.s2.b5: The shamans built their reputations as voices of God by sprinkling and naming the newborn and presiding over burials. Through fees they grew wealthy, became the original aristocracy exempt from tribal restrictions, and suppressed rivals by branding them witches. Even so, the author fairly adds that the veneration of shamanism shows the premium mankind placed on wisdom.
p090.s3.h: III. The Shamanic Theory of Disease and Death — From Ghosts to Natural Causes
p090.s3.b0: Ancient man believed that he and his material surroundings responded directly to the whims of ghosts and spirits, so his religion was almost wholly concerned with material affairs. Since all disease and death were regarded as spirit phenomena, it was inevitable that the shaman, besides being priest, should also labor as doctor and surgeon.
p090.s3.b2: These theories bore directly on human lives. Some primitive peoples still kill someone whenever a nonviolent death occurs, the medicine man naming the guilty party; obscure deaths were laid to witchcraft and a supposed witch executed. The note that ancient coroner’s inquests, which dissected the body to settle the cause of death, saved many such lives shows that the search for facts is itself a way of saving people.

p090.s3.b4: This list is a ladder of thought by which mankind has tried to explain suffering. The observation that the fourth theory—disease as punishment for personal or racial sin—still prevails among reputedly civilized groups invites us to examine how we look upon a sick neighbor. An understanding of old age and contagion is gradually erasing the fear of ghosts and gods as the authors of human misery.
p090.s3.b6: The author explains that evolution instills a superstitious fear of the unknown as the scaffolding for the God concept, and then, once revelation has brought a better comprehension of Deity, sets in motion forces of thought that inexorably remove the scaffolding. The decline of superstition is not a crisis of faith but the taking down of a scaffold that has served its purpose.
p090.s4.h: IV. Medicine under the Shamans — Faith and Secrecy
p090.s4.b0: The entire life of ancient men was prophylactic, and their religion was in no small measure a technique of disease prevention. They had unbounded faith in their remedies, and that faith was itself a powerful remedy. The author observes that the faith needed to recover under an ancient shaman was not much different from the faith needed to experience healing at the hands of some of his later-day, nonscientific successors.
p090.s4.b2: For long ages primitive tribes feared the sick and shamefully neglected them. Later the whole clan would crowd into the sickroom to help the shaman howl the disease ghosts away, and sometimes a woman diagnosed while a man treated. Through mistaken theories—such as the belief that every animal-caused disease had its beneficent plant remedy—mankind slowly groped its way toward real medicines.

p090.s4.b4: The Greeks were the first to evolve truly rational methods of treating the sick, and both Greeks and Egyptians received their medical knowledge from the Euphrates valley. Many secret remedies lost their power once they became known.
p090.s5.h: V. Priests and Rituals — A Millstone, and Leaders Who Pointed the Way
p090.s5.b0: For the savage, the essence of ritual was the perfection of its performance. Done correctly, it compelled the spirits; done wrongly, it angered the gods. So the early shamans inevitably evolved into a priesthood trained to direct meticulous ritual, and for tens of thousands of years endless rituals were an intolerable burden on every act of life.

p090.s5.b3: Priests specialized according to their natural talents, and when religion became institutionalized they claimed to “⟦Q 90:5.5⟧hold the keys of heaven.⟦/Q⟧” This claim shows the secondhand religion described in the introduction at its height: the authority of the intermediary who stands between man and God.
p090.s5.b4: Words like amen and selah, pilgrimages, purification rites, and prayer, song, and responsive reading all belong to this lineage of ritual. Interestingly, the habit of swearing is explained as a prostitution of the old ritual repetition of holy names. Priests sought to awe the people with an ancient tongue and magical passes in order to enhance their own authority.
p090.s5.b6: The author’s judgment is balanced. The priesthoods delayed scientific development and hindered spiritual progress, yet they contributed to the stabilization of civilization and to certain kinds of culture.
p090.s6.b0: Paper 90 shows that on religion’s road from fear to love there was a long age when intermediaries stood in the way. Shamans and priests laid burdens on people through trickery and monopoly, but they also left a tradition of caring for the sick and honoring wisdom. For today’s reader the paper asks whether anyone’s special mediation is really needed to reach God, and whether ritual has quietly taken the place of religion in our own faith.

p090.s6.b2: The next paper, Paper 91, “The Evolution of Prayer,” shows how prayer that began as incantation and bargaining grows into spiritual communion and worship, completing this series on primitive religion.
p091.lead: From a muttered wish for luck to communion with the indwelling Adjuster: the evolutionary road of prayer, and the conditions of effective praying.

p091.foot.text: Presented by the Chief of the Urantia Midwayers

p091.s0.b0: Paper 91 completes the series on primitive religion, which ran from the ghost cult to shamanism, with the subject of prayer. Its author, the Chief of the Urantia Midwayers, explains that prayer as an agency of religion evolved from earlier nonreligious monologue and dialogue. When primitive man became self-conscious, other-consciousness inevitably followed, carrying a twofold potential: social response and the recognition of God.
p091.s0.b1: The earliest prayers were not addressed to Deity at all; they were much like saying to a friend before some important undertaking, “⟦Q 91:0.2⟧Wish me luck.⟦/Q⟧” This muttered wish for luck widened into ceremonies of friends, family, and clan; when ideas of ghosts and spirits arose, it was addressed to superhuman beings; and with the consciousness of gods it rose at last to genuine prayer. The author illustrates prereligious praying with the Toda tribe and the mana practices of the Melanesians.
p091.s1.h: I–II. Primitive Prayer; Evolving Prayer — An Agency for Conserving Values
p091.s1.b0: The function of early evolutionary religion is to conserve and augment social, moral, and spiritual values, and this is chiefly done through prayer. Because prayer was allied only with values that had group approval, a person seeking antisocial ends had to turn to magic and sorcerers rather than prayer. Prayer therefore became, very early, a mighty promoter of social evolution and moral progress.
p091.s1.b2: Primitive man prayed for food, rain, and game. The author calls this a perversion of prayer, yet credits it with raising the mores, since it encouraged people to pursue material goals through social and ethical action. Among the dangers of prayer he lists a morbid sense of sin, along with ignorance, superstition, crystallization, devitalization, materialism, and fanaticism.
p091.s1.b3: Prayer moved from verbalized wishes to a technique of gaining spirit co-operation, and then to the higher function of conserving all worth-while values. When man learned that prayer could not coerce the gods, it became petition and favor seeking. The idea of sacrifice weakens true prayer, because people offer material possessions in place of their own consecrated wills; and when religion loses a personal God, its prayers turn into theology and philosophy.
p091.s1.b5: For the average person prayer is largely an exchange with his own subconscious, but the spiritually progressing individual attains some contact with the superconscious levels of the mind, the domain of the indwelling Thought Adjuster. Beyond that there is also a definite spiritual phase in which prayer is received and recognized by the spiritual forces of the universe.
p091.s2.h: III. Prayer and the Alter Ego — From Fiction to Reality
p091.s2.b0: Children learning to speak think out loud, and when imagination dawns they converse with imaginary companions. This ability to turn monologue into a pseudo dialogue is the psychological root of prayer. Much of an adult’s thinking, too, is carried on in conversational form.

p091.s2.b2: The author says that from the first conceiving of an alter ego to the concept of a heavenly Father, prayer has always been a socializing, moralizing, and spiritualizing practice. Even apart from its spiritual side, ethical prayer is a splendid way to elevate and reinforce the self; it sends the ego looking both ways for help—downward to the subconscious reservoir of experience, upward to the superconscious borders where the Mystery Monitor makes contact.
p091.s2.b4: The most practical counsel of this section is that enlightened prayer must recognize not only an external, personal God but also the internal Divinity, the indwelling Adjuster. As primitive man spoke to a near-by alter ego, so we may now speak directly with that alter ego, knowing that it is no fiction but the presence of God dwelling within us.
p091.s3.h: IV–V. Ethical Praying; Social Repercussions of Prayer
p091.s3.b0: No prayer can be ethical when it seeks selfish advantage over others; such praying slips back into primitive pseudo magic. The author advises us not to expect God to love us more than our friends, neighbors, or even enemies. When a prayer seeks nothing for the one who prays or for anyone else, the soul tends toward true worship.
p091.s3.b2: Materialistic praying breeds disillusionment as science reveals a universe of law, yet even such petitions are somewhat effective because they lead to efforts that help bring about their answers. The spiritually advanced should therefore be very cautious about discouraging the prayers of the immature.
p091.s3.b4: Prayer echoes beyond the individual into society. A group praying together for moral uplift makes every member better, and confession, repentance, and prayer have led whole cities and nations to reform. Prayer also holds the remedy for a critical habit.
p091.s3.b6: The social effect grows when the person prayed for knows of it and the one praying comes into close contact with him. Prayer also gives rise in time to secondary agencies such as priests, holy books, and rituals; those who are God-conscious without symbols must be patient and tolerant toward those who need them. The strong must not look with disdain upon the weak.
p091.s4.h: VI. The Province of Prayer — What It Can and Cannot Do
p091.s4.b0: Prayer has no direct effect on the physical environment unless it is linked with the will of the spiritual forces and material supervisors of a realm. Nor is it a technique for curing organic disease. Yet it has contributed enormously to abundant health and to the cure of many mental, emotional, and nervous ailments, has added to the efficacy of other remedies, and has turned many a complaining invalid into a paragon of patience.
p091.s4.b1: Apart from its religious meaning, prayer is a sound psychological practice for realizing the reserve powers stored in the unconscious mind. The author urges us, however hard it may be to reconcile scientific doubts with the urge to seek divine help, never to forget that the sincere prayer of faith is a mighty force for happiness, self-control, social harmony, and spiritual attainment.
p091.s4.b3: The rest of the sentence restores the balance: never hesitate to ask God for wisdom and spiritual strength while you yourself courageously attack the problems at hand. With the counsel to pray as Jesus taught—honestly, unselfishly, with fairness, and without doubting—the author stresses that the efficacy of prayer does not depend on knowledge, social level, or culture; every person can reach through prayer the threshold of contact with the Adjuster.
p091.s5.h: VII. Mysticism, Ecstasy, and Inspiration — Tested by the Fruits
p091.s5.b0: Mysticism, as a technique of cultivating the consciousness of God’s presence, is praiseworthy, but when it leads to social isolation and fanaticism it is all but reprehensible. What the overwrought mystic takes for divine inspiration is too often the uprising of his own deep mind. Contact with the Adjuster is favored by meditation but more frequently facilitated by loving, unselfish service to others.

p091.s5.b3: Genuine spiritual ecstasy is usually accompanied by great outward calmness and emotional control. The warning not to mistake every vivid presentiment or intense emotion for revelation, and the remedy that the dangers of overmuch private, aesthetic praying are corrected by group praying and community devotions, apply directly to spiritual life today.
p091.s6.h: VIII–IX. Praying as a Personal Experience; Conditions of Effective Prayer
p091.s6.b0: Prayer is spontaneous. Long before he had a clear concept of God, primitive man reached out for help in dire need and burst into expressions of joy when jubilant. The author makes plain that prayer did not evolve from magic; each arose independently.

The author says we should be unafraid to talk to God, but that trying to persuade or change God is the attitude of a spiritual child. Genuine prayer does attain reality; it adds to spiritual growth and modifies attitudes.
p091.s6.b5: God answers prayer by giving an increased revelation of truth, an enhanced appreciation of beauty, and an augmented concept of goodness. Words are merely the intellectual channel through which the river of spiritual supplication may flow.

p091.s7.b0: Paper 91 shows that prayer is not a descendant of magic but, from its own separate root, the effort to adjust personality to the will of God. Prayer that began as a muttered wish for luck can grow into communion with the indwelling Adjuster. Prayer does not change God but changes the one who prays; it does not replace action but inspires it. So the paper asks less about the theory of prayer than about the attitude of a praying life.

p091.s7.b2: The next paper, Paper 92, “The Later Evolution of Religion,” shows how evolutionary religion, having grown this far, meets revelation and advances to higher levels.
p092.lead: From fear to love: the merits and faults of evolutionary religion, the five epochal revelations, the great religious leaders, and the religions of the twentieth century.

p092.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p092.s0.h: Introduction — Three Ministries That Raised Up Evolutionary Religion
p092.s0.b0: Paper 92 follows the earlier papers on primitive religion and the origin of prayer and sums up the course religion took afterward. Its author, a Melchizedek of Nebadon, begins by noting that man possessed a **religion of natural origin** long before any systematic revelation. That religion grew out of man’s superanimal endowments and developed slowly through influences working within, and upon, savage, barbarian, and civilized man alike.

head: Ministry
What it does
rows: 1. The adjutant of worship

2. The adjutant of wisdom

3. The Holy Spirit
The initial supermind bestowal — the capacity to realize the postulate of survival in concept and experience

p092.s0.b2: The co-ordinated working of these three ministries is quite sufficient to begin and carry forward evolutionary religion. Much of the potential of these divine agencies has never yet found expression, and much will be revealed as mortal religion ascends. Here the paper lays down its basic outlook: religion is neither merely man-made nor simply dropped from above.
p092.s1.h: I. The Evolutionary Nature of Religion — From Fear to Love
p092.s1.b0: Religion began with fear and ghosts and passed through stages of first coercing and then cajoling the spirits. Fetishes grew into totems and tribal gods; magic formulas became prayers. Having moved from nature worship through ghost worship to fetishism, mankind, the author judges, is now approaching maturity and ripening for real religion and the revelation of truth itself.
p092.s1.b1: Religion is the last thing to perish or change in a race, and as a social institution it embraces rites, symbols, scriptures, altars, and temples. Its basic stimulus has always been fear. As civilization advances, fear is softened by reverence, admiration, respect, and sympathy, and then further conditioned by remorse and repentance.
p092.s2.h: II. Religion and the Mores — An Institution That Clings to the Old
p092.s2.b0: Religion is the most rigid and unyielding of human institutions, yet it eventually reflects the changing mores. Because it regards the ancient as sacred, it clung to old forms such as altars of unhewn stone, primitive fire drills, and unleavened bread. The author adds a word of advice: when modern readers are puzzled by things in old scriptures, they should remember that later generations feared to remove what their ancestors held holy.
p092.s2.b1: Nor can religious growth be hurried. A people absorbs from an advanced religion only what fits its own evolutionary status, and it outwardly accepts a new faith while actually adjusting it to its old mores. The author then draws an important line concerning conscience.
p092.s2.b3: Conscience is merely the sum of the moral content of the mores of its time, and untaught by experience and unaided by reason, it can never be an unerring guide. This passage can be read as counsel not to equate our convictions with the will of God, but to test them continually by experience and reason.
p092.s3.h: III. The Nature of Evolutionary Religion — Costly but Effective
p092.s3.b0: The study of religion is like examining the fossil-bearing social strata of the past. Evolutionary religion has been preoccupied with rites and dogmas, often tainted by the chosen-people delusion, and its cardinal ideas—atonement, sacrifice, salvation, and the rest—go back to the age of primordial ghost fear. Unlike science, it makes no provision for its own correction, so revision must always be forced on it from outside.
p092.s3.b2: Only two influences can uplift natural religion: the pressure of slowly advancing mores and the periodic illumination of epochal revelation. The author records the merits and faults of evolutionary religion with balance.

p092.s3.b5: So we must be careful when criticizing evolutionary religion. It is what actually happened, a historical fact, and it is the sacred heritage of animal ascent, which must ever be refined by the censorship of revealed religion and the fiery furnace of genuine science.
p092.s4.h: IV. The Gift of Revelation — Five Epochal Revelations
p092.s4.b0: Revelation too is progressive. It sorts and censors the religions of evolution, but because teaching too far removed from the thought of the age would not be received, it is always limited by man’s capacity of receptivity. Revealed religions are marked by belief in a Deity of final value and in the survival of personality after death.

p092.s4.b3: It is striking that the fifth revelation, these papers themselves, admits its own incompleteness. No revelation short of the attainment of the Universal Father can ever be complete, and all other celestial ministrations are partial and transient. This candor, offered even at the risk of weakening its authority, asks the reader not for blind belief but for a reflective faith.
p092.s5.h: V. The Great Religious Leaders — Seven Religious Epochs since Adam
p092.s5.b0: Most great religious epochs have been launched by the life and teachings of some outstanding personality. People tend to venerate the leader even more than his teachings, because of an instinctive longing for help from above. That longing was designed to anticipate the Planetary Prince and the Material Sons; deprived of them, Urantia has tried to make good the loss by wrapping its human leaders in legends of supernatural origin.

p092.s5.b2: The author finds the greatness of Moses in his wisdom and sagacity: others had greater concepts of God, but no one ever succeeded in leading so many people to adopt such advanced beliefs. The section closes with the hope that future teachers will work less to strengthen interreligious barriers and more to build a brotherhood of spiritual worship among the followers of differing theologies.
p092.s6.h: VI. The Composite Religions — The Religions of Twentieth-Century Urantia
p092.s6.b0: The religions of the twentieth century offer an interesting study of the social evolution of the worship impulse. Some groups remain close to the ghost cult; others have long held to monotheism. Evolutionary and revealed religion are progressing side by side, blending into diverse theologic systems, which the author lists as eleven.

p092.s6.b2: The text sketches each briefly. The Hebrew religion is the link between the religions of evolution and those of revelation; Buddhism has shown remarkable adaptability to the mores of many peoples; Christianity, after Paul, became so thoroughly Occidentalized that many non-European peoples see it as a strange revelation for strangers. From the difficulty Mohammed’s followers had with the doctrine of the Trinity comes a general principle: it is always hard for evolutionary minds to accept advanced revealed truth suddenly.
p092.s7.h: VII. The Further Evolution of Religion — Unity in Worship
p092.s7.b0: Religion can never become a scientific fact, nor can new religions be invented; they are either evolved or revealed, and the old is never lost but merged with the new. On this principle the author sets out a standard for the relations among religions.
p092.s7.b2: For any group to regard its creed as The Truth bespeaks theological arrogance. Since every faith contains truth, it is far better to borrow the best in a neighbor’s living faith than to denounce the worst in his lingering superstitions. Religions can never achieve uniformity of creeds and rituals, but they can, and someday will, realize unity in true worship of the Father of all.

p092.s7.b4: A child’s religious experience depends greatly on whether fear or love dominated the relationship with its parents. The author regrets that those who venerate the risen Christ have overlooked the man—the valiant and courageous hero Joshua ben Joseph. Modern man must make more readjustments of values in one generation than were made in two thousand years, and so religion must be redefined.
p092.s8.b0: Paper 92 looks on the long history of religion with a fair eye. It hides neither the superstitions nor the harm of evolutionary religion, yet acknowledges it as the most effective institution that sustained civilization, and it says that revelation too is given progressively, within the limits of human receptivity. Its conclusion is a call to humility and respect toward other faiths, and to grow into a religion of love rather than fear.

p092.s8.b2: The next paper, Paper 93, “Machiventa Melchizedek,” tells in detail how Melchizedek of Salem—introduced here as the third epochal revelation—came to Urantia and what he taught.
p093.lead: An emergency Son who came in human form to keep the fading light of truth alive: the story of Machiventa Melchizedek, the sage of Salem, of Abraham, and of the covenant of faith.

p093.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p093.s0.b0: The previous paper named Melchizedek of Salem as the third of Urantia’s five epochal revelations. Paper 93 introduces in detail the one who brought it. The Melchizedeks are widely known as **emergency Sons**, because when an extraordinary problem arises or something unusual is to be attempted, it is quite often a Melchizedek who takes the assignment; they have the peculiar ability to function even on the physical level of personality manifestation.
p093.s0.b1: The Melchizedeks have been exceedingly active on Urantia. One corps of twelve served with the Life Carriers, and after the Caligastia secession a later corps of twelve became receivers for the planet. These receivers returned after the default of Adam and Eve and remained in charge until Jesus became the titular Planetary Prince. Machiventa was one of these twelve receivers.
p093.s1.h: I. The Machiventa Incarnation — A Self-Chosen Emergency Bestowal
p093.s1.b0: In the millenniums after the miscarriage of the Adamic mission, revealed truth was threatened with extinction. Mankind progressed intellectually but slowly lost ground spiritually, and by about 3000 B.C. the idea of God had grown very dim. The receivers knew that Michael’s bestowal was coming, but not how soon.
p093.s1.b2: They appealed to the Most Highs of Edentia and then to the Father Melchizedek, but were told only to uphold truth in the manner of their own election. So Machiventa volunteered to do what had been done only six times in all the history of Nebadon: to personalize on earth as a temporary man of the realm. The story shows the responsibility of finding a way forward from one’s own post when not everything is settled from above.
p093.s2.h: II. The Sage of Salem — Ninety-Four Years as a Man
p093.s2.b0: Machiventa was materialized, unseen by human eyes, 1,973 years before the birth of Jesus. He was first observed when he entered the tent of Amdon, a Chaldean herder, and that evening he ate material food for the first time. His whole mission was contained in his first words.
p093.s2.b2: He soon became known as the priest of El Elyon and the sage of Salem, and Salem later became Jerusalem. His body resembled a human one, but it was unique in several ways.

p093.s3.h: III–IV. Melchizedek’s Teachings; The Salem Religion — Favor Gained by Faith
p093.s3.b0: Melchizedek founded schools at Salem patterned on the old system of the Sethite priests. He taught one universal God, yet allowed people to associate this teaching with the Most High of the constellation of Norlatiadek. To most he taught no more than that, while to gifted disciples such as Nordan the Kenite he taught even the truths of the superuniverse and Havona. He taught each person only as much as he could receive.
p093.s3.b1: But he subordinated everything to the doctrine of one God, the universe Deity and divine Father. He also taught that another Son of God would come, born of a woman, and so prepared the way for Michael’s bestowal. Salem worship was very simple: each believer memorized and subscribed to three beliefs.

p093.s3.b3: Even this brief creed was too advanced for the people of that day. So convinced were they that man was born under forfeit to the gods that they could not grasp the idea of divine favor given freely, by faith. Melchizedek therefore offered a sacrament of bread and wine in place of blood sacrifice, but he never succeeded in fully uprooting the urge to sacrifice.

p093.s3.b6: Like Jesus, Melchizedek attended strictly to the mission of his bestowal. He did not set out to reform the mores or spread scientific knowledge, but concentrated on two tasks: to keep alive the truth of the one God and to prepare the way for the bestowal of a Paradise Son.
p093.s4.h: V–VI. The Selection of Abraham; Melchizedek’s Covenant with Abraham — From Conquest to a Spiritual Kingdom
p093.s4.b1: Salem was chosen for two reasons. Palestine was then central to the world’s trade, travel, and civilization, and thus well suited for Michael’s later appearance; and there contact could be made with the children of Terah, marked by intelligence, initiative, and sincerity. Terah’s family had been half converted in Ur through the preaching of Ovid, and Abraham came to Salem with his nephew Lot.
p093.s4.b2: Abraham, however, had kingly ambitions. He confederated seven tribes, defeated the petty kings who had raided Lot’s property, and gave a tenth of the spoils to Salem. Melchizedek, who was not militaristic, accepted a defensive policy but would not approve of conquest.
p093.s4.b3: When Abraham came to him, troubled that he had no son to succeed him, Melchizedek persuaded him to give up material conquest for the spiritual concept of the kingdom of heaven. Then, bidding him number the stars, he made a formal covenant with him.
p093.s4.b5: When Isaac was born, Abraham had the covenant put in writing and changed his name from Abram to Abraham. After the reconciliation he again took up the civil and military leadership of Salem and greatly improved its school and missionary work. The text portrays him as a shrewd and efficient businessman—not overly pious, but thoroughly sincere, and one who truly believed in Melchizedek.
p093.s5.h: VII. The Melchizedek Missionaries — A Gospel Submerged
p093.s5.b0: The Salem missionaries went to Egypt, Mesopotamia, and Asia Minor, and from Lake Van onward to Europe, the British Isles, Iceland, China, and Japan. The text honors their lives as a heroic chapter in the annals of the human race. Yet outside Palestine the idea of one God never claimed the continued allegiance of a whole tribe or race, and the gospel was absorbed into older cults such as those of the Great Mother and the Sun.
p093.s6.h: VIII–IX. Departure of Melchizedek; After Melchizedek’s Departure — The Forgotten Teacher
p093.s6.b0: Shortly after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Machiventa decided to end his bestowal. The chief reason was that people were beginning to regard him as a demigod and to revere him with superstitious fear; he also wished to leave while Abraham was still living, so that the truth would become firmly established in his followers’ minds. One night he said good night, retired to his tent, and in the morning was gone.
p093.s6.b1: Abraham never fully overcame his grief at losing his teacher, and for a time he became fearful and timid. Even so, he again became the spiritual leader of Palestine and died confident in the faith he had learned from Melchizedek. In later generations the story came to seem a myth, but Joseph firmly believed in Melchizedek and chose civil administration over command of the Egyptian armies.
p093.s6.b2: The text explains that what the Old Testament describes as conversations between Abraham and God were really conferences between Abraham and Melchizedek, and that during the editing in the Babylonian captivity the records were altered and most traces of Melchizedek erased. As a result his teaching about the promised bestowal Son was also lost, and very few recognized Michael when he came. The passage shows how easily the preservation of truth can fail.
p093.s7.h: X. Present Status of Machiventa Melchizedek — An Open Future
p093.s7.b0: On the third day after his disappearance from Salem, Machiventa appeared among his eleven fellows and resumed his career as a planetary receiver. His coming and going were marked by no special announcement and no resurrection roll call. Yet he did not leave the flesh until he had been released by the Father Melchizedek and his bestowal approved by Gabriel.

Such prospects make Urantia one of the most interesting and intriguing spheres in all of Nebadon.

The covenant in which God promises to do everything and man agrees only to believe reads as an invitation to receive salvation as a gift, not a bargain. At the same time, Abraham’s ambition and fear, and the slow forgetting of the truth, show that the road of faith is never smooth.

p093.s8.b2: The next paper, Paper 94, “The Melchizedek Teachings in the Orient,” examines how the teachings the Salem missionaries carried to India, China, and beyond met and were changed by the religions there.
p094.lead: The Salem gospel in India and China: its encounters with the Vedas and Brahmanic philosophy, Hinduism, Lao-tse and Confucius, Gautama and Buddhism.

p094.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p094.s0.h: Introduction — The Salem Missionaries Go East
p094.s0.b0: Where Paper 93 told of Machiventa’s work at Salem, Paper 94 follows his teaching as it spread eastward. The Salem teachers carried to the remotest tribes of Africa and Eurasia the gospel that faith and trust in the one universal God is the only price of divine favor. They worked by training native converts and sending them out as teachers among their own people.
p094.s0.b2: The paper evaluates the religions of the East, but by a consistent standard: how close each tradition came to the Salem gospel of a personal God and salvation by faith, and what it missed. It should therefore be read both as a comparison and as an expression of respect for the high achievements of each tradition.
p094.s1.h: I–II. The Salem Teachings in Vedic India; Brahmanism — A Gospel Rejected
p094.s1.b0: In Melchizedek’s day India had recently come under the rule of Aryan-Andite invaders from the north and west. Their polytheism was a degeneration of an earlier monotheism, as each tribe came to venerate its own god, and the many gods were being reorganized into a pantheon under Dyaus pitar, Indra, and Agni. The one God preached by the Salem missionaries was not wholly out of harmony with the emerging idea of the Father-Brahma, but the nonritualistic Salem doctrine ran directly counter to the Brahman priesthood.
p094.s1.b1: To combat the Salem teachers, the Brahmans compiled the sacred writings of their day, which became the basis of the Rig-Veda. The text judges that the Vedas at their best equal any comparable writings, yet as they mingled with countless cults they became the most variegated system of theology ever developed by mortal man.
p094.s1.b2: As the caste system hardened, the priestly caste went so far as to set itself alongside the gods. The doctrine of transmigration, which came from the Deccan, robbed people of the old hope of deliverance and advancement in death, and it led on to the doctrine of an eternal escape from self. The author weighs this course gravely.
p094.s1.b4: In the age when the Brahmanas and Upanishads were compiled, the Brahmans tried to remove human elements from their concept of deity and fell into the error of depersonalizing God. In the same period Buddhism arose, but after a thousand years of success it gave way in northern India.
p094.s2.h: III. Brahmanic Philosophy — Speculation That Stopped Short of Truth
p094.s2.b0: The text counts the highest phase of Brahmanism among the most noble reaches of the mortal mind into philosophy and metaphysics. Yet its speculation never took up the essential dual concept of religion: the existence of the Universal Father and the ascending experience of creatures who seek him. Brahman was an Absolute understood only by negating every finite quality, and so it had almost no personal attributes that an individual could experience.

p094.s2.b2: The decisive flaw was the failure to distinguish levels of reality: what may seem illusory on the absolute level may be absolutely real on the finite level. Brahmanism also failed to take account of the personality of the Universal Father, who is personally contactable on all levels.
p094.s3.h: IV. The Hindu Religion — The Most Adaptive Faith
p094.s3.b0: Over the centuries the people of India returned largely to the Vedic rituals as crystallized by the Brahman priesthood. The text calls Hinduism the oldest and most cosmopolitan of the world’s religions and notes that present-day Hindu theology depicts four descending levels of deity.

p094.s3.b2: Hinduism’s strength lies in its general tolerance and its flexibility, embracing everything from lofty speculation to simple folk practice. Having no great hierarchy, it survives because it is woven into the daily life of the people. The author says that India already has the philosophical framework and the cult structure; what it needs is the original gospel of Jesus, freed from Western dogma—a brotherhood realized in loving ministry and social service.
p094.s4.h: V–VI. The Struggle for Truth in China; Lao-Tse and Confucius
p094.s4.b0: The Salemites reached China in the middle of the second millennium before Christ and for more than a hundred years kept their headquarters at See Fuch, training Chinese teachers. The direct result was early Taoism, a religion vastly different from the one bearing that name today.

p094.s4.b2: This belief became known in Japan as Shinto, and in China it blended with ancestor worship. Since Singlangton the Chinese had never been enslaved to priestcraft and so were early freed from abject fear of the gods, but the text judges that they went no further and fell into ancestor worship. Still, the Salem seed was not sown in vain; it became the root of the great philosophers of the sixth century.
p094.s4.b3: In the sixth century before Christ, when Melchizedek’s teachings were in danger of being submerged, the Salem gospel was restated through several human teachers. Lao-tse, building on the Salem traditions, declared Tao to be the One First Cause of all creation, taught that man’s destiny was everlasting union with Tao, and gave one of the earliest presentations of returning good for evil.
p094.s4.b5: Confucius built on the better moral traditions of the yellow race and put morality in the place of magic. His writings became the moral basis of the culture of almost a third of Urantians, though he is also judged to have made a new fetish of order and somewhat stifled the spirit of investigation. In the end both men were deified by their followers.
p094.s5.h: VII–VIII. Gautama Siddhartha; The Buddhist Faith
p094.s5.b0: In the same century Gautama Siddhartha arose in India. He was heir to the throne of a petty chieftain of a small mountain valley; he fought the caste system and turned people from seeking salvation through physical affliction. He did not grasp the personality of the One Universal, but after his pupil Bautan told him of the Salem traditions, he took an advanced stand on salvation through faith.
p094.s5.b2: His gospel of universal salvation, free from priests and sacrifice, came surprisingly near to a revival of the Salem gospel. Yet his son, in later years, wavered about divine favor through faith alone. Gautama’s original gospel can be summed up in a simple profession and a few teachings.

p094.s5.b5: The text finds Gautama’s great truth in his proclamation of a universe of absolute justice, and calls his philosophy the ideal humanism, which removed the grounds for superstition and fear of ghosts. Its great weakness was that it did not produce a religion of unselfish social service. Even so, Gautama’s life was much greater than his preaching.
p094.s6.h: IX–X. The Spread of Buddhism; Religion in Tibet
p094.s6.b0: Buddhism represented the Melchizedek truths better than any other religious system in eastern Asia. King Asoka trained and sent out more than seventeen thousand missionaries in twenty-five years, and in one generation made Buddhism the dominant religion of half the world.
p094.s6.b2: But the farther it spread, the more Buddhism became a miraculized gospel that made Gautama a god. In the south the Hinayana clung to the early doctrine, while in the north the Mahayana cast off its social limitations. Today Buddhism remains a living religion that promotes calmness, self-control, and serenity.
p094.s6.b3: In Tibet the Melchizedek teachings are found in the strangest combination with Buddhism, Hinduism, Taoism, and Christianity. The text judges that the resulting ritual has become inordinately cumbersome, and sums it up this way.
p094.s7.h: XI–XII. Buddhist Philosophy; The God Concept of Buddhism
p094.s7.b0: The great advance of Buddhist philosophy was its grasp of the relativity of all truth. Teaching that small truth is for little minds and large truth for great minds allowed Buddhists to reconcile differences both within their own scriptures and with other religions. The teaching that the Buddha nature resides in all men is likewise counted among the clearest expressions of the truth of the indwelling Adjuster.

p094.s7.b3: Such concepts helped intellectuals unify their philosophy, but the text says that even an anthropomorphic Yahweh has greater religious value than a remote Absolute, for the multitudes hungered for the promise that faith in God would assure divine favor and survival. That hunger finally bore fruit in Japan in the belief in Amida Buddha, which taught salvation by faith in the mercy of Amida.
p094.s7.b4: The text names Buddhism’s freedom to choose truth from all religions as its great strength and looks with hope to its twentieth-century renaissance. The paper then closes with a sentence addressed to the peoples of every faith.
p094.s8.b0: Paper 94 shows both the heights and the limits of the religions of the East. The deep speculation of Brahmanic philosophy, the insight of Lao-tse, and the sincerity of Gautama all touched the Salem gospel, and the way their teachings were clouded by deification and ritualism is something Western religion has experienced as well. The purpose of the comparison is not to rank religions but to train the eye to recognize the core—a personal God, faith, and service—wherever it appears.

p095.lead: The Salem gospel in the Levant, cradle of Western faith: failure in Mesopotamia, Egypt’s moral culture with Amenemope and Ikhnaton, Zoroaster in Iran, and Arabia.

p095.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p095.s0.h: Introduction — The Levant, Cradle of Western Faith
p095.s0.b0: Where Paper 94 followed the Salem gospel eastward, Paper 95 traces its western road. As India gave rise to the religions of eastern Asia, so the Levant was the homeland of the faiths of the Occidental world. The Salem missionaries spread through Palestine, Mesopotamia, Egypt, Iran, and Arabia, but the results differed from land to land.

p095.s1.h: I. The Salem Religion in Mesopotamia — Attempting Too Much
p095.s1.b0: By 2000 B.C. Mesopotamia had almost lost the teachings of the Sethites. The Salem teachers reduced the chief gods to seven—Bel, Shamash, Nabu, Anu, Ea, Marduk, and Sin—and then exalted Bel, Ea, and Anu as a supreme triad of earth, sea, and sky. These triads were based on the Salemites’ belief in Melchizedek’s insignia of the three circles.
p095.s1.b1: Things went wrong when Nabodad, leader of the school at Kish, launched a concerted attack on temple harlotry. When the social reform failed, the spiritual teachings went down with it, and the cult of Ishtar and astrology enjoyed a great revival. The author names the cause of the failure plainly.
p095.s1.b3: The missionaries had been commissioned to preach a definite gospel, but they became entangled in the apparently worthy cause of reforming the mores. The lesson is to hold to the central mission and not let side causes drain one’s strength. Even so, scattered bands kept faith in the one Creator, and the psalms they inscribed on stone later found their way into the Hebrew collection of hymns. The text adds that the Book of Job fairly reflects the teachings of the Salem school.
p095.s2.h: II. Early Egyptian Religion — From Tombs to Conscience
p095.s2.b0: The original Melchizedek teachings took their deepest root in Egypt. Egypt fostered the most thoroughly blended religious philosophy, and the Jews took their idea of creation from Babylon but their concept of divine Providence from Egypt. Egypt was more favorable to the Salem teaching because each dynasty exalted its tribal god as creator of all others, accustoming the people to the idea of a supergod.
p095.s2.b1: Seeing that bodies buried in the sand were preserved, the Egyptians began to embalm the dead, and burial statues led to great advances in art. Magical texts such as The Book of the Dead appeared, but in the Nile valley ritual early became bound up with conscience and character. So, in time, the Egyptians came to rely for salvation on ethical ideals rather than elaborate tombs.
p095.s2.b2: When Melchizedek appeared, the Egyptians had a religion far above that of their neighbors. They believed the soul came to the judgment hall of Osiris and, if innocent of murder, robbery, falsehood, adultery, theft, and selfishness, entered the realms of bliss. The idea of judgment after death for one’s earthly life passed from Egypt into Hebrew theology.
p095.s3.h: III. Evolution of Moral Concepts — The Humanism of the Nile
p095.s3.b0: Much of Egypt’s social and ethical idealism grew up in the Nile valley as a purely evolutionary development. Here the author states an important principle: moral evolution does not depend wholly on revelation; because a divine spirit indwells him, man can derive spiritual values and cosmic insight from his own experience.
p095.s3.b3: Yet Egypt was intellectual and moral but not overly spiritual. Of the four great prophets who arose in six thousand years, Amenemope was followed for a season, Okhban was murdered, Ikhnaton was accepted halfheartedly for one generation, and Moses was rejected. Even so, the teachers of the Nile valley were the first to proclaim conscience as the mandate of God.
p095.s4.h: IV. The Teachings of Amenemope — A Link to the Hebrews and Greeks
p095.s4.b0: Amenemope, whom many called the “⟦Q 95:4.1⟧son of man⟦/Q⟧,” exalted conscience as the highest arbiter between right and wrong. He believed God-consciousness to be the determining factor in all conduct and that every moment should be lived aware of God’s presence and of responsibility to him. The text says his instruction to his son on honesty in public office would do honor to any modern statesman.

p095.s4.b3: Amenemope was not the greatest religious teacher of his age, but he was the most influential, passing on the ethics of evolution and the morals of revelation both to the Hebrews, among whom Western religious faith reached its peak, and to the Greeks, who carried pure philosophy to its greatest heights.
p095.s5.h: V. The Remarkable Ikhnaton — A Reformer Too Far Ahead
p095.s5.b0: As Amenemope’s teachings were losing their hold, a woman of the royal family, influenced by a Salemite physician, persuaded her son Ikhnaton to accept the doctrine of One God. The text says that no one since Melchizedek had possessed so clear a concept of the Salem religion, and that Ikhnaton kept open the philosophic monotheistic channel needed for Michael’s bestowal. The child Jesus was taken to Egypt partly in recognition of this achievement.
p095.s5.b1: Under the guise of sun-god worship, he led people to worship the One God, creator of Aton. He wrote a thirty-one-chapter book, “⟦Q 95:5.7⟧The One God,⟦/Q⟧” and one hundred and thirty-seven hymns, and made “righteousness” the supreme word of daily life. In that generation neither social position nor wealth gave any Egyptian an advantage before the law.

p095.s5.b3: His son-in-law changed his name to Tutankhamen and went back to the old gods. Yet the idea of one God never died out, and the democracy of salvation and resurrection that Ikhnaton taught eventually prevailed. The repercussions of his work persisted for centuries in Palestine and Greece.
p095.s6.h: VI. The Salem Doctrines in Iran — Zoroaster
p095.s6.b0: The Salem teachers made headway in Iran for more than five hundred years, until a change of rulers brought persecution that all but ended their teaching. Then, in the sixth century before Christ, Zoroaster appeared to revive the smouldering embers. On a pilgrimage to Ur he had learned the traditions of Caligastia and the Lucifer rebellion and of the Seven Master Spirits, and he created a galaxy of seven supreme gods with Ahura-Mazda at its head.
p095.s6.b1: His was a religion of action—work—rather than prayers and rituals, a militant philosophy that dared to battle evil, inaction, and backwardness. Zoroaster did not teach fire worship but used the flame as a symbol of the wise Spirit; his later followers worshiped the symbol. Nor was the original teaching a pure dualism.

p095.s7.h: VII. The Salem Teachings in Arabia — Failure Close to Home
p095.s7.b0: Not even in China or Rome did the Melchizedek teachings fail more completely than in the Arabian desert, so very near Salem itself. Each tribe worshiped its fetish and each family its household gods, and rival concepts of deity contended for ages. Some clans clung to a hazy idea of the one God, and many centers might have responded to the gospel of Jesus, but the Christian missionaries of the desert were austere and unyielding.
p095.s7.b1: The author says that had the followers of Jesus been more gracious in their preaching and less stringent in social requirements of their own devising, many lands, Arabia among them, would gladly have received the simple gospel of the carpenter’s son. Instead, the tribes’ common reverence for the black stone at Mecca became the point of contact for the later establishment of Islam. The text finds Islam’s strength in its clear presentation of Allah as the one Deity, and its weakness in spreading by military force and in its degradation of woman.
p095.s8.b0: Paper 95 shows through many examples that the way truth is shared matters as much as the truth itself. Mesopotamia failed by attempting too much, Ikhnaton by moving too fast, Arabia by being too rigid. Egypt’s moral culture, on the other hand, testifies that people can reach high ideals through experience even before revelation.

p095.s8.b2: The next paper, Paper 96, “Yahweh—God of the Hebrews,” describes how the concept of God evolved among the Hebrew people, into whom all these streams flowed.
p096.lead: From the tribal god of the Horeb volcano to the loving Creator Father: the Hebrew concept of God, which grew while keeping the same name, and the leadership of Moses.

p096.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p096.s0.b0: Paper 96 describes how the concept of God grew among the Hebrew people, into whom the many streams of the Levant flowed. The author first lays out, in three stages, the general path by which man conceives of Deity. Not only the Hebrews but also the Hindus and Mesopotamians followed a similar road, and ideas of monotheism matured all over the world not long after Melchizedek appeared at Salem.

p096.s0.b2: The Salem religion survived as a tradition among the Kenites and other Canaanite tribes, and when the Hebrews adopted it, it was enriched by Egyptian morals, Babylonian theology, and Iranian ideas of good and evil. This had a clear purpose: Michael could hardly come to Urantia until there existed a people believing in the Universal Father among whom he could appear.
p096.s1.h: I. Deity Concepts among the Semites — Many Names, One Stream
p096.s1.b0: The early Semites believed that everything was indwelt by a spirit, and Melchizedek’s teaching never fully destroyed this belief. The Hebrews’ progress from polytheism through henotheism to monotheism was not unbroken; it suffered many retrogressions. To avoid confusion, the author first defines the various titles of Deity.

p096.s1.b2: Until about 2000 B.C. Mount Sinai was an intermittently active volcano, and its fire, smoke, and thunder made the Bedouins greatly fear Yahweh. For a long time the Hebrews believed other gods existed but held them subordinate to Yahweh. Yet this concept went through a remarkable development.
p096.s1.b4: As the Buddha concept led at last to the Universal Absolute, the Yahweh concept led finally to the idea of the Universal Father. Strikingly, while the Jews changed their view from the tribal god of Mount Horeb to the loving and merciful Creator Father, they never changed his name; they went on calling him Yahweh. The passage shows that understanding can keep growing under the same name.
p096.s2.h: II. The Semitic Peoples — The Making of the Clans of Israel
p096.s2.b0: Racially the Semites were among the most blended of peoples, carrying hereditary factors from almost all of the nine world races. The Arabian Semites repeatedly fought their way into the northern lands and were repeatedly driven out, and during a severe famine they entered Egypt as contract laborers, only to undergo the bitter experience of enslavement.
p096.s2.b1: The text makes clear that Abraham was not the racial father of all the Hebrews. His offspring coming out of Egypt formed the nucleus, but most of those who joined the clans of Israel had never been in Egypt; they were fellow nomads who chose to follow Moses. During the captivity the Melchizedek covenant was largely forgotten, and the religion of the common people was the old Yahweh ritual of magic and sacrifice.
p096.s3.h: III. The Matchless Moses — Organizer of a Forlorn People
p096.s3.b0: Moses’ mother was of the royal family of Egypt, and his father was a Semitic liaison officer between the government and the Bedouin captives. His ancestry was so blended that he cannot be classified in any one race, and that very versatility and adaptability enabled him to lead a diverse horde. He chose to leave the culture of the Nile kingdom and cast his lot with his father’s people.
p096.s3.b2: Moses first sought freedom through diplomacy. He made a compact with the king for a peaceable departure, but when the king repudiated it, Moses was not discouraged; he bided his time. When the Egyptian army was tied up resisting Libyan and Greek attacks at once, he led his people out in a carefully planned night flight. Patience in waiting for the right moment after a setback was one side of his leadership.
p096.s4.h: IV. The Proclamation of Yahweh — A New Concept in an Old Name
p096.s4.b0: Moses had heard Melchizedek’s teachings from his parents, was raised to believe in El Shaddai, and through his Kenite father-in-law came to believe in El Elyon. From all these he formed an enlarged concept of Deity, and judging that the slaves would never grasp the idea of El Elyon, he wisely decided to proclaim it as an expanded concept of their old tribal god, Yahweh.
p096.s4.b1: This left Moses always in an awkward predicament, trying to present a new and higher idea under an ancient name long symbolized by the golden calf. During the long stay before Sinai the ten commandments were given and the ceremonial worship refined, and the violent eruption of Horeb in the third week impressed upon the people a God who was a devouring fire.
p096.s4.b3: Under Moses the tribal nature god Yahweh became the Lord God of Israel, and later, through the Babylonian captivity, the concept was freed to take on the monotheistic role of the God of all nations. The author finds the most unique feature of Hebrew religious history in this continuous evolution from the primitive god of Mount Horeb to the loving and merciful Creator Father proclaimed by the Isaiahs.
p096.s5.h: V. The Teachings of Moses — A Lofty Vision and the People’s Level
p096.s5.b1: The Hebrews had no written language at the time of the exodus, so the record of Moses’ deeds was drawn from traditions more than a thousand years after his death. Much of his advance over neighboring religions was due to the Kenite traditions of Melchizedek’s time. Moses and his father-in-law Jethro gathered up those remnants, joined them with Egyptian learning, and organized the Hebrew ceremonial system of worship.

p096.s5.b3: The author says it was truly pitiful to watch this great mind trying to adapt his sublime concept of El Elyon to the understanding of the ignorant. Moses feared to proclaim the mercy of Yahweh and preferred to awe his people with the fear of God’s justice. As a result, when he passed on, the tribes quickly reverted to the worship of the golden calf. Even so, he had welded thousands of wanderers into a self-sustaining nation and handed them over to Joshua.
p096.s6.h: VI. The God Concept after Moses’ Death — An Opportunity Nearly Lost
p096.s6.b0: After Moses died, his lofty concept rapidly deteriorated. The leaders kept the tradition, but the people slipped back into the old desert ideas, and the backward drift continued under the Judges. The change from nomadic herders to settled farmers demanded a change in their concept of God, and in that transition the Hebrews nearly lost monotheism altogether.
p096.s6.b1: This was not merely one people’s loss. They nearly lost the opportunity to be the vital link that would preserve the Melchizedek teaching until the incarnation of a bestowal Son. Joshua preached a stern gospel to stem the tide, and even in this dark age solitary teachers arose to proclaim again the Mosaic concept of God.
p096.s7.h: VII. Psalms and the Book of Job — A Light Kept at Ur
p096.s7.b0: Once settled in Palestine, the Hebrews were contaminated by less advanced Canaanite practices, and their idea of God fell far below the concepts maintained by surviving Salem groups in Egypt and Mesopotamia. Those higher concepts are recorded in some of the Psalms and in the Book of Job.

p096.s7.b3: In Palestine the wisdom and all-pervasiveness of God were often grasped, but seldom his love and mercy. Only at Ur did a voice arise—Elihu, prophet of Ur and priest of the Salem believers—to proclaim a God gracious to the repentant, salvation by faith. Not since Melchizedek had the Levant heard so cheering a message.
p096.s7.b5: Thus the remnants of the Salem missionaries in Mesopotamia kept the light of truth burning while the Hebrews were disorganized, until the long line of Israel’s teachers arose, building concept upon concept until they reached the ideal of the Universal and Creator Father of all.
p096.s8.b0: Paper 96 shows that the concept of God was not completed all at once but grew little by little through a people’s experience and the labors of its leaders. Moses had a lofty vision yet had to meet the people at their level, and he left behind both the cost and the value of that compromise. The central message of the paper is that, even under the same name, our understanding of God can grow from fear into love.

p097.lead: From a tribal deity to the loving Father of all mankind: how the Hebrew prophets, from Samuel to the second Isaiah, enlarged the God concept, and how the priests rewrote the record.

p097.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p097.s0.h: Introduction — A God Made Less Human but Not Abstract
p097.s0.b0: Paper 97 follows the concept of Yahweh after Moses, the subject of the preceding paper, as it grew in the hands of the Hebrew prophets. Its author, a Melchizedek of Nebadon, credits the spiritual leaders of the Hebrews with something no one before them had achieved. They stripped their God concept of its human form without turning it into an abstraction that only philosophers could grasp.
p097.s0.b2: The thread running through the whole paper is the concept of the **personality of God**. Clearly taught at Salem in the days of Melchizedek, it had grown vague and hazy by the time of the flight from Egypt. From Moses to Malachi it then grew almost without a break, until it was heightened and glorified at last in Jesus’ teaching about the Father in heaven.
p097.s1.h: I. Samuel—First of the Hebrew Prophets — The Changeless God
p097.s1.b0: Pressure from the surrounding peoples drove the Hebrew tribes to unite under a centralized government, and this gave Samuel, who came from a long line of Salem teachers, his field of work. He was a man of action more than of preaching, rough enough to overthrow a score of Baal sites in a single day. His success was only partial: he won back to the higher concept of Yahweh only the more intelligent half of the Hebrews.
p097.s1.b1: Samuel’s great contribution lay elsewhere. People of his time pictured Yahweh as a fitful God of jealous whims, forever regretting what he had done. Samuel declared instead that Yahweh was changeless, the source of all truth, stability, and constancy. He also proclaimed that the Lord raises the poor out of the dust, a word that shocked those who measured divine favor by material prosperity and gave new hope to thousands of the despairing poor.
p097.s1.b3: His limits were real as well. Samuel did not progress very far beyond the concept of a tribal god, and his idea of mercy at first extended only to those who were themselves merciful. His successors could not keep his pace, and the keynote of the era was **divine power**, preached in support of the king upon the Hebrew throne.
p097.s2.h: II–III. Elijah and Elisha; Yahweh and Baal — A Struggle over the Land
p097.s2.b0: After the nation split into two kingdoms, Elijah restored to the northern kingdom a concept of God comparable with that of Samuel’s day, and Elisha, with the help of the little-known Micaiah, kept that light alive. The author sums up the period, however, not as a time of progress in the concept of Deity but as one of recovery, regaining ground that had been lost.
p097.s2.b1: Especially striking is the paper’s reading of the long contest between Yahweh and Baal. At first, it explains, this was less a difference in religious belief than a socioeconomic clash over the ownership of land.

p097.s2.b3: When Ahab had the Naboths murdered in order to seize their land, Elijah made a moral issue out of the olden land mores. From then on the land question became a religious one, Yahweh against Baal, and the prophet who began as an agrarian reformer ended by exalting Deity.
p097.s3.h: IV. Amos and Hosea — The God of Justice, the God of Love
p097.s3.b0: Amos was no mere restorer; he was a discoverer of new concepts of Deity. He proclaimed that Yahweh would no more tolerate crime and sin among his own people than among any other, and so, for the first time since Melchizedek, denounced the double standard of national justice and morality. This struck directly at the idea of the “chosen people” as a privilege. He warned that ritual must not take the place of righteousness, and he was stoned to death for his courage.
p097.s3.b1: Hosea followed Amos’s God of justice and revived the Mosaic concept of a God of love. He preached forgiveness through repentance, not by sacrifice, and his message was always one of hope. The author contrasts the two: Amos quickened the national conscience to justice, while Hosea struck the opening notes of the divine compassion that Isaiah would later sing.
p097.s4.h: V–VI. The First Isaiah; Jeremiah the Fearless — Beyond Ritual, Beyond Nation
p097.s4.b0: The first Isaiah preached the eternal nature of God, his infinite wisdom, and his unchanging reliability, and he carried the promise that sins as scarlet would become white as snow. Micah and Obadiah, who followed him, fearlessly attacked the priest-ridden sacrificial system. Micah’s message still reads today as a short summary of what religion is about.
p097.s4.b2: Jeremiah took the next step in the internationalization of Yahweh. He declared that Yahweh did not take the side of the Hebrews in their wars but was God of all the earth and of all nations. For counseling surrender during the siege of Jerusalem he was cast into a miry pit, yet through him the concept of Yahweh rose to a level of planetary and even cosmic dignity.
p097.s5.h: VII. The Second Isaiah — The Highest God Concept before Jesus
p097.s5.b0: In the Babylonian captivity the priests reshaped the national history to restore the nation and glorify its traditions. The paper fairly adds that they did not claim inspiration or profess to be writing a sacred book; they were preparing a textbook to bolster the courage of their fellow captives. Into this setting came a young prophet, the second Isaiah, whose writings survive in chapters forty to fifty-five of the book of Isaiah.
p097.s5.b1: The author judges that no teacher from Machiventa to the time of Jesus reached a concept of God as high as the second Isaiah’s. He proclaimed the Creator of the universe as the affectionate Father of all mankind, and in doing so effectively eclipsed the nationalistic Yahweh.
p097.s5.b2: His God was no small, man-made deity. God’s ways and thoughts are as far above ours as the heavens are above the earth, yet this same God calls each person by name and engraves his children on the palms of his hands. Preaching by the river in Babylon to listeners of many nations, the second Isaiah worked to correct racially egoistic ideas of the Messiah’s mission, though the priests’ nationalism kept him from full success.

p097.s6.h: VIII–IX. Sacred and Profane History; Hebrew History — A Rewritten Record
p097.s6.b0: The author points out that the custom of treating one people’s record as sacred history and the rest of the world’s as profane history has caused much confusion. According to the paper, the priests of the Babylonian exile, after preparing their new record, destroyed the existing accounts of the doings of the kings. Five hundred years of foreign rule, and the conflicting promises of deliverance offered by the prophets, then threw the honest Jew into deep perplexity.
p097.s6.b1: At the root lay an oversimplified view of Providence: righteousness is rewarded and sin is punished. The paper reads the drama of Job as a protest against this philosophy and the pessimism of Ecclesiastes as a worldly wise reaction to it. The disappointment born of hopes dashed again and again finally left the leaders unable to recognize the One who came as the Son of Man.
p097.s6.b3: Section nine rereads the main points of Hebrew history in this light, and some of its examples are listed below. The author’s conclusion is that this history is not a chronicle of miracles but ordinary profane history. That does not belittle the people’s spiritual contribution: Judaism was the soil out of which Christianity grew.

p097.s6.b5: The captivity shocked the remnant into monotheism. In Babylon the Jews concluded that they must convert the gentiles, and from this came a new concept of destiny: that they were to become the chosen servants of Yahweh. The doctrine of immortality also took form there, and religion began to take shape as a system of thought more and more separate from politics and economics.
p097.s7.h: X. The Hebrew Religion — What Kept It Alive
p097.s7.b0: Their leaders taught that to be chosen meant not a monopoly of divine favor but the special service of carrying the truth of the one God to every nation. Yet after the return from exile the people chose the rules and rituals of the priesthood and rejected the magnificent concept of the second Isaiah. Even so, an unbroken line of faithful teachers passed the monotheistic torch from Moses to John the Baptist.

p097.s7.b2: The remark about institutions is especially worth pondering today. Religion finds it hard to survive as the private practice of isolated individuals. Rather than tearing down all ritual on seeing the evils of institutional religion, it is better to reform it, and in this the author considers Ezekiel wiser than his contemporaries.
p097.s8.b0: Paper 97 calls the change from the barbaric idea of the jealous spirit of the Sinai volcano to the concept of the loving and merciful Father of all mankind the greatest feat in the evolution of religion ever achieved on Urantia. It came not through a single revelation but through generations of teachers each taking one step further. Since a person’s own understanding of God grows in much the same way, this paper is both the story of a people and a map of our own growth.
